# Writing style — comments, help text, and CLI output

This file is the house style for everything a reader sees: Go doc comments,
`--help` output, and the strings a command prints or returns as errors. It
applies to every Go file in this repository. Keep it short enough that it can
be re-read before every PR.

---

## Code comments

**Explain why, not what changed.** A comment answers the question the code
cannot: the invariant, the trade-off, the reason a non-obvious choice is the
safe one. It never narrates history.

- Never reference a PR, issue, fix, or the past tense of the code itself.
  "Used to", "now", "previously", "after the refactor", "fixes #123" are all
  forbidden. Git history already knows; the reader of the code does not care.
- A doc comment on every exported symbol. One or two sentences is usually
  enough. `golint` enforces this; don't make a reviewer do it.
- Target ≤ 10 lines per doc block. If you need more, the extra content
  belongs in `docs/` or a README, not above the function.
- "Deliberately not X" comments are encouraged when they stop a plausible
  wrong refactor. `internal/gitops/remote.go` is the exemplar: it says the
  function is *not* used to derive the cache directory, and why.
- No TODO, FIXME, HACK, or XXX in committed code. File an issue instead.

---

## Help text (cobra)

`--help` is reference material, not a blog post. A reader in a terminal wants
to know what the command does, what it costs, and which flags change the
behavior. Philosophy and motivation belong in `docs/`.

- **`Short:`** one line, imperative verb, no trailing period.
  Good: `Pin a component's image digest into an environment`
  Bad:  `This command pins the image digest.`
- **`Long:`** target ≤ 150 words, hard ceiling ~200. Cover: what it does,
  what it reads, what it writes, what can go wrong that the user can prevent.
  Cut: why the command exists, why GitOps is good, architecture essays.
- **`Use:`** positional args in `<>`, optional in `[]`, variadic as `name...`.
  Good: `pin <component> [version]`
  Bad:  `pin COMPONENT [VERSION]`, `pin <component> [<version>]`

If a `Long:` draft exceeds 200 words, the excess is almost always the second
paragraph onwards. Move it to a file under `docs/` and keep the help text
to usage.

---

## Flag descriptions

Use the shared constants in `cmd/intropy/flagtext.go`. Never hand-write a new
description for a flag another command already has:

- `--output`, `--env`, `--gitops-repo`, `--argocd-server`, `--domain`,
  `--system`, `--template-version` all have constants.
- If you add a flag that several commands will share, add a constant first.
- Flag descriptions are fragments, not sentences: no trailing period, no
  "This flag…". Start with the noun. Good: `target environment (required)`.

---

## Runtime output

A CLI's output is read twice: once by a human scanning, once by a script
parsing. The two never share a stream.

- **stdout is for results.** Tables, JSON, the thing the command was run to
  produce.
- **stderr is for everything else.** Progress, warnings, completion messages,
  errors. A pipeline reading stdout must never see a status line.

### Voice

- Progress and completion: **lowercase, present tense, no trailing period**.
  Good: `syncing api on argocd.example.com at a1b2c3d`
  Good: `published ghcr.io/example/releases/api:1.2.0`
  Bad:  `Published ghcr.io/…`  `Sync complete.`
- Empty states follow the same rule: `no releases found`, not
  `No releases found.`
- A follow-up hint naming a command goes on its own line, in backticks:
  `use 'intropy release create <component>' to publish one`

### Errors

- Front-load what failed. The remediation, if there is one, goes on a second
  line. Do not editorialize — the user is already reading an error.
  Good: `pending change is a1b2c3d, not the f4e5d6c you reviewed`
        `run 'intropy deploy diff api --env staging' before syncing`
  Bad:  `…has advanced since you reviewed it — you really should read the new diff…`
- Wrap errors with context as they travel up: `fmt.Errorf("pull %s: %w", …)`.
  The outermost prefix names the command or operation, not the internals.

### Vocabulary

- **image digest**, not "bits", "artifacts", or "the images".
- **environment** in prose, `--env` only when naming the flag.
- A template's message **direction** is derived from its block kind: an
  extractor publishes, a loader subscribes, a transactional integration
  wires no messages. The flags follow it: `--publishes` for producing
  templates, `--subscribes` for consuming templates.
- **message** is a message definition: a registry entry (`message list`,
  `message show <ref>`) or a producing component's `publishes` declaration.
  A subscription is written to the record as a `subscribe` block; a
  producer's as `publishes`. **event** is prose for the runtime occurrence
  of a message, never a scaffold value. `contract` survives only where the
  .NET shared-project type name is literally meant — transitional.
- `->` for a transition (`1.0 -> 1.1`), ` @ ` for a pin (`api @ 1.2.0`).
  Never mix the two in one message.
- A commit SHA is shown short (7 chars) unless the full value is the point.

### Command verbs

One verb per meaning, used on every noun (`int`, `template`, `deploy`, ...).
The full set, grouped by what the verb does to the world:

**Read-only** — exit 0 even when the answer is "they disagree", never write
to git, never trigger a sync:

- **`list`** enumerates a collection: integrations on disk, templates in the
  library, published releases. It never prints one item's
  details.
- **`show`** prints the details of exactly one thing: a template's manifest,
  an integration's scaffold record. It never enumerates.
- **`status`** reports one component across every environment, one row
  each, and whether the rows agree. It never prints one environment's
  details — that is `show`.
- **`diff`** prints the rendered change a `sync` would apply, as the
  resources themselves. Both sides are committed revisions; it never diffs
  an uncommitted worktree.
- **`inspect`** prints the deployment model derived from one system topology:
  components, workloads, ports, and available local fixtures. It never
  renders manifests or writes project or Git state.
- **`render`** emits a complete Kubernetes YAML stream for one environment.
  It may ask for missing local fixture choices, buffers and validates the whole
  stream before writing stdout, writes all interaction and diagnostics to
  stderr, and never changes project, Git, or cluster state.

**Create or change project state** — may write files under the project.
Manifest creation may push a review branch, never the default branch:

- **`create`** makes something new from a template or from scaffolded
  parts: an integration, a system host, a release manifest to publish, or
  missing Kubernetes manifests on a GitOps review branch. Manifest creation
  accepts existing identical files but never replaces or deletes a file.
- **`add`** attaches something that already exists elsewhere to this
  project: a library registration. Unlike
  `create`, the content is pulled, not generated.

# intropy-atrium

Two portals per customer, from one repository:

- **Intropy Atrium**, the developer portal: the integration landscape for developers,
  built from each system's topology. [Web UI](web/README.md)
- **Atrium Hub**, the customer portal: how the customer's integrations are running,
  for their IT, in plain words (decision 0009). [Web UI](customer-web/README.md)

Both are served by the Go code in [backend](backend/README.md). See also the
[design](docs/design.md) and the [decisions](docs/decisions/).

## Run it

Everything runs through [Task](https://taskfile.dev) (`brew install go-task`). Every
project has a Taskfile with the same verbs, whatever its stack, so `task dev` works
the same for Go, npm or, later, .NET:

| Verb    | Does                                            |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `setup` | install dependencies                            |
| `dev`   | run it locally, with whatever it needs started  |
| `test`  | run the tests                                   |
| `check` | types, formatting, vet: what CI should fail on  |
| `build` | produce the artefact                            |

From the root they run for every project (`task test`), or for one with a prefix
(`task backend:test`, `task web:dev`). `task` alone lists everything.

```sh
task dev          # Postgres, the API on :8080 and the UI on :5173
task seed         # in another terminal: load the demo systems
task dev:mock     # or: only the UI, with the in-browser mock API
task dev:hub      # Atrium Hub: its API on :8090 and UI on :5180 (after task seed)
```

`task dev` asks you to sign in: a mock identity provider on :8180 stands in for
Entra, and any username works (`backend/dev/README.md`).

Needs Go 1.26+, Node 22+ and Docker (for Postgres and the mock identity provider).

A new project gets its own Taskfile with the same verbs and an `includes` entry in
the root `Taskfile.yml`.

## Image

Each portal is one distroless image with its API and UI (decision 0008), built from
the root Dockerfile:

```sh
task image        # atrium:dev, the developer portal
task image:hub    # atrium-hub:dev, the customer portal
task image:run    # run atrium:dev on :8081 against the local Postgres
```

## Helm chart

`deploy/helm/atrium` installs both portals, with schema migrations as a pre-sync Job.
See its [README](deploy/helm/atrium/README.md).

```sh
task chart:lint   # lint, render and validate
task chart:try    # install into a throwaway kind cluster and check it end to end
```

## CI and releases

GitHub Actions, as in business-incident-service:

- **CI** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`), on pushes to main and pull requests: the
  backend's formatting, vet and tests (with a Postgres, so the store tests run),
  both UIs typechecked and built, both images built, and the chart linted and
  validated.
- **Release** (`.github/workflows/release.yml`), when a GitHub release is published.

### Releasing

A release is a GitHub release with a tag `vX.Y.Z` on main. Publishing it builds and
pushes, all as `X.Y.Z`:

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Atrium's image | `harbor.intropy.io/platform/atrium:X.Y.Z` |
| Atrium Hub's image | `harbor.intropy.io/platform/atrium-hub:X.Y.Z` |
| The chart (its version and appVersion) | `oci://harbor.intropy.io/platform-charts/atrium`, and attached to the release |

```sh
gh release create v0.1.0 --target main --generate-notes             # a release
gh release create v0.2.0-rc.1 --target main --generate-notes --prerelease
```

The chart installs the images of its own version, so a GitOps repo pins one
number: the chart's. A full release also moves the images' `latest` tag; a
pre-release doesn't. A tag that isn't `vX.Y.Z` (or `vX.Y.Z-rc.N`) fails the
release before anything is pushed.

The jobs run in the `release` environment, which only `v*` tags may use, with
the repository secrets `HARBOR_USERNAME` and `HARBOR_PASSWORD`.

# Intropy Atrium — design

## Status

Draft (2026-11-10). Open for review.

## Goal

Give each customer one place to see everything about their integrations. The first
goal is an **integration catalog**: the systems, components and messages declared in
each system's topology, shown in a hosted web UI.

Over time the portal becomes a single pane for the integration landscape, with
read-only views into the tools around it: secret names in OpenBao or Azure Key Vault,
Sluicio, CI, ArgoCD and others. How those views work is deliberately left undecided
here. This document only makes sure the catalog does not block them.

## Context

`intropy dashboard` already renders a catalog locally. It finds every system host in
the workspace and runs the host's `graph` verb (`dotnet build`, then
`dotnet run -- graph`) to get the declared topology. That is right for a developer's
machine. It does not suit a shared, hosted view:

- It needs a .NET SDK and a checkout of every system repository.
- A cold build takes minutes per host.
- It shows the working tree, not what is merged or deployed.

The portal therefore gets the topology from CI and serves it from its own store.

## Principles

- **Complement the CLI, never replace it.** The CLI and the local dashboard stay as
  they are, and nothing moves out of the CLI. See
  [0001](decisions/0001-complement-the-cli.md).
- **Read-only, with two exceptions.** The portal shows state and does not change it,
  which rules out approvals and workflows of its own. The exceptions are writing a new
  version of a secret, without ever reading a value (see
  [0005](decisions/0005-write-only-secrets.md)), and starting a promotion, which runs
  the CLI in the GitOps repository's CI rather than in the portal (see
  [0006](decisions/0006-promote-through-ci.md), proposed).
- **The topology document is the contract.** The portal and the CLI share no code.
  Both read the JSON that the `Intropy.Topology` `graph` verb emits.
- **The catalog is the spine.** Systems, components, messages and environments are
  entities with stable identities, so later views have something to attach to.

## Scope

### First version

- Topology delivery from CI on merge to the main branch.
- Ingest and storage of topology snapshots per system and commit.
- A read API for systems, components and messages.
- A web UI with a catalog list and an entity page laid out so more views can be added.
- Sign-in with Entra ID: the customer's directory and Integrio's (0011).
- Deployment to one cluster through GitOps.

### Not in the first version

- Views from other tools (secrets, Sluicio, CI, ArgoCD and others).
- "What is deployed in each environment". The first version shows the latest topology
  on the main branch.
- Authorization beyond "signed in", such as per-system access.
- Any write action.

## Architecture

```
system repo CI ──POST topology──▶  ┌─ Atrium image ─────┐
                                   │  API (Go)  /api/…  │ ──▶  Postgres
                     browser ────▶ │  UI files  /…      │
                                   └────────────────────┘
                                             │
                                       Entra ID (OIDC)
```

- **Deployment.** One portal per customer, in the customer's cluster, covering all of
  that customer's environments. See [0002](decisions/0002-one-portal-per-customer.md).
  The Helm chart `deploy/helm/atrium` installs both portals; schema migrations run in
  a pre-sync Job with their own database user.
- **Backend.** Go: the same language as the CLI and the rest of the platform tooling.
- **Datastore.** Postgres: a Postgres operator in-cluster, or Azure Database for
  PostgreSQL when running in Azure. See [0004](decisions/0004-postgres.md).
- **UI.** A separate frontend application that talks only to the portal API. The API
  serves its built files, so one distroless image runs both on one origin. See
  [0008](decisions/0008-one-image.md).
- **Authentication.** Both portals sign people in with OpenID Connect against the
  providers each install lists: the customer's Entra tenant and Integrio's. Roles
  come from the providers' claims; sessions are cookies. See
  [0011](decisions/0011-identity.md).

## Atrium Hub

The customer portal, for the customer's IT, is a separate product: `cmd/atrium-hub`
and `customer-web/`, its own image and deployment, reading Atrium's database through
a read-only user (0009). Its catalog is built around integrations (0010). For now it
is one page: the integrations, their status, and links to Revision and Sluicio, which
the customer's IT already uses. Its API:

- `GET /api/config`: the product name and whether incidents are on.
- `GET /api/integrations`, `GET /api/integrations/{id}`: each integration's name,
  description, contact, what it reads from and writes to (business systems, or other
  integrations), and links to its diagram in Revision and its messages in Sluicio.
- `GET /api/incidents?from=…&to=…`: incidents in a period, per integration affected.

## Topology delivery

See [0003](decisions/0003-ci-pushes-topology.md).

The CI workflow that intropy-templates generates gets a step that, on merge to the main
branch:

1. builds the system host and runs its `graph` verb;
2. posts the resulting document to the portal, along with the system name, commit,
   ref and repository.

Because the step lives in the templates, every new system feeds the portal without
extra setup. Ingest is idempotent on system and commit, so re-running CI is safe and
can be used to backfill.

## Data model

- `topology_snapshot`: system, commit, ref, repository, received time, the raw
  document and the docs CI sent, as JSONB; primary key system and commit. The raw
  document is kept so new fields can be read later without re-running CI.
- The catalog is projected in Go on each read, from the latest snapshot per system
  (`backend/internal/catalog`). With a handful of systems per customer that's a few
  milliseconds, and it keeps one place that decides what a document means. Projected
  tables (`system`, `component`, `message`, `message_endpoint`) can come when a
  cross-system query needs them.

## API (sketch)

- `GET /api/config`: the install's feature flags; every source but the topology is
  optional (see [0007](decisions/0007-optional-sources.md), proposed).
- `POST /api/topologies`: ingest, called by CI.
- `GET /api/systems`, `GET /api/systems/{system}`
- `GET /api/systems/{system}/topology`: the latest snapshot's document as CI posted it,
  which the system graph draws.
- `GET /api/components/{component}`
- `GET /api/messages`, `GET /api/messages/{message}`
- `GET /api/systems/{system}/revision`, `GET /api/components/{component}/revision`: what
  Revision knows around the entity (description, attributes, diagrams, neighbours) and
  about the system's external systems.
- `GET /api/systems/{system}/docs`: the repository's `README.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` from the
  latest snapshot, as raw Markdown. CI sends them in the same `POST /api/topologies`
  request as a `docs` field (`[{ "path": "RUNBOOK.md", "content": "…" }]`), so docs always
  match the topology's commit. No build step; the UI renders the Markdown.
- `GET /api/secrets`: every secret's name and version metadata per environment, with
  what uses it: the Dapr components that reference it (`secretKeyRef`) and the app
  components those are scoped to, read from the manifests in the GitOps repository.
- `GET /api/incidents?from=…&to=…`: production incidents from incident.io that overlap
  the period, with the components each affected and how (degraded, partial outage,
  full outage). The UI turns them into daily status and uptime per system and
  component.
- `GET /api/components/{component}/secrets`: the secrets a component can use, through
  the Dapr components it's scoped to.
- `POST /api/secrets`, `POST /api/secrets/{secret}/{environment}/versions`: create a
  secret, write a new version; responses hold metadata only.
- `GET /api/components/{component}/promotions`: the component's runs of the GitOps
  repository's `promote` workflow, read from the git provider.
- `POST /api/components/{component}/promotions` (`{ "from": "test", "to": "prod" }`):
  starts that workflow, which runs `intropy deploy promote`. The response is the run.

## Open questions

- **CI authentication to the ingest endpoint.** A shared token per customer is the
  simplest option. GitHub Actions OIDC federated with Entra avoids storing a secret.
- **The deployed view.** Showing what runs in each environment likely means joining
  GitOps pins (image digests) with release manifests (digest to commit) and the
  snapshot for that commit. Topology is per system while releases are per component,
  so the join needs a rule for choosing a system's commit.
- **Authorization.** Whether everyone with a role sees everything, or groups map to
  systems. Today there is one role per portal (`developer`, `viewer`).
- **Who may write secrets and start promotions.** Likely a role per environment
  (from an app role or group, 0011), with prod narrower than dev and test, matching the promote workflow's
  environment protection rules. Also where the audit record lives: the store's audit
  log and the workflow runs may be enough.
- **Which secrets should exist.** Listing what is in the store is easy. Showing a
  secret as missing needs the expected names, which the Dapr components'
  `secretKeyRef`s in the GitOps repository give, per environment overlay. Also open:
  the store path layout (the mock uses `kv/intropy/<env>/<secret>`), and whether Dapr
  components shared across systems live in a shared namespace.
- **Matching entities to Revision.** The mock matches systems and components on a
  Revision component `ref` of `intropy/<system>[/<component>]`, and external systems on
  name. The Revision docs don't say whether `ref` is returned on reads, so check that
  first. Revision has no webhooks, so the backend polls and caches.
- **Where integrations are declared** (0010): tags in the system hosts' code, a YAML
  file in the GitOps repository, or Revision. A JSON file for now.
- **Matching incidents to components.** The mock assumes each incident.io incident lists
  affected catalog components. In incident.io that's likely a catalog type for Intropy
  components, synced from Atrium, and a custom field or status page components on the
  incident. Also: whether uptime should count partial outages fully, as now, or
  weighted, as some status pages do.
- **Which snapshot is latest.** The latest is the last one received. Backfilling an
  older commit after a newer one would make the older one current; ordering by commit
  needs the git history, or CI sending the commit time.
- **Topology schema drift.** The portal has its own Go types for the document. A JSON
  Schema published with `Intropy.Topology` would let both the CLI and the portal
  validate against one definition.

## Plan

1. Portal repository: the Go service with ingest, schema, read API and Entra sign-in.
   Ingest, schema, the catalog read API, docs and sign-in are in `backend/`.
2. CI step in intropy-templates that posts the topology.
3. UI: catalog list and entity page.
4. Deploy to an internal environment through GitOps, then to one customer.

The first version is done when a merge in a system repository shows up in that
cluster's portal without anyone touching it.
# Atrium backends

Two services from one Go module, sharing the domain packages:

- `cmd/atrium`, Intropy Atrium's API: CI posts each system's topology, and the API
  serves the catalog the developer UI reads. Postgres stores the snapshots (0004).
- `cmd/atrium-hub`, Atrium Hub's API, the customer portal (0009): integrations,
  business systems and incidents, read-only. See [Atrium Hub](#atrium-hub) below.

```sh
task backend:dev       # Postgres in Docker, then the API on :8080
task backend:seed      # post the demo topologies, as CI would
task backend:test      # unit and HTTP tests
task backend:test:db   # plus the store, against the local Postgres
```

## Configuration

All from the environment, so the same binary runs locally and in a cluster. The
Taskfile sets local defaults; set a variable in your shell to override it.

| Variable              | Default (Taskfile)        | Meaning                                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ATRIUM_DATABASE_URL` | the compose Postgres      | Postgres connection string (required)                      |
| `ATRIUM_INGEST_TOKEN` | `REDACTED`               | bearer token CI sends; unset turns ingest off              |
| `ATRIUM_FEATURES`     | `docs`                    | optional sources to turn on; unset is the catalog only     |
| `ATRIUM_ADDR`         | `:8080`                   | where to listen                                            |
| `ATRIUM_WEB_DIR`      | unset (image: `/srv/web`) | the built UI to serve at `/`; unset serves the API only    |
| `ATRIUM_LOG_FORMAT`   | `text` (binary: `json`)   | log format                                                 |
| `ATRIUM_MIGRATE`      | `true`                    | `false` when a separate job runs `atrium migrate` (the Helm chart does) |
| `ATRIUM_APP_ROLE`, `ATRIUM_HUB_ROLE` | unset      | the roles the portals run as; migrating grants each its rights (Atrium: data; the hub: read, plus `session`) |
| `ATRIUM_AUTH_CONFIG`  | `dev/auth-atrium.json`    | the sign-in providers (see Sign-in); required unless auth is off |
| `ATRIUM_SESSION_KEY`  | a fixed local key         | encrypts the cookie that carries a sign-in through the provider; 32+ characters, the same on every pod |
| `ATRIUM_AUTH`         | unset                     | `off`: no sign-in, everyone is a developer. Demos only      |

`ATRIUM_FEATURES` takes the names in decision 0007 (`docs,deployments,…`), or `all`.
A source this build doesn't serve yet stays off with a warning, so the UI never asks
for an endpoint that isn't there. Today that's everything except `docs`.

## Sign-in

Decision 0011: both services sign people in themselves with OpenID Connect
(`internal/auth`), against each provider in `ATRIUM_AUTH_CONFIG`:

```json
{
  "baseUrl": "https://atrium.acme.example",
  "providers": [
    {
      "id": "customer", "name": "Acme",
      "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0",
      "clientId": "<app registration>", "clientSecretEnv": "ATRIUM_OIDC_CUSTOMER_SECRET",
      "roleClaim": "roles", "roles": { "Atrium.Developer": "developer" }
    }
  ]
}
```

Each provider is a button on the sign-in page; callbacks go to
`<baseUrl>/auth/callback/<id>`. Roles come from the `roleClaim` claim (default
`roles`) through that provider's `roles` map, plus its `defaultRole` if set; someone
with no role is signed in but gets 403. `baseUrl` and issuers must be https (except
localhost), and issuers a single tenant, never Entra's `common`.

Sessions are rows in Postgres (`session`); the cookie holds a random token whose
SHA-256 is the row's key. A session ends after an hour unused, eight hours after
sign-in, at sign-out, or when its provider's issuer, client or role mapping changes.
Revoking is deleting rows: `delete from session where provider = … and subject = …`.
Atrium Hub writes its sessions there too, so its otherwise read-only user needs
insert, update and delete on `session`; migrating grants that when `ATRIUM_HUB_ROLE`
names it. Signed-in API responses are `no-store`.

Locally `task backend:dev` starts a mock OIDC server on :8180 playing two directories,
`customer` and `integrio`; [dev/README.md](dev/README.md) says what to type.

## Endpoints

| Endpoint                                | Feature  |
| --------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `GET /api/config`                       | always, no sign-in |
| `POST /api/topologies`                  | always, the ingest token instead of sign-in |
| `GET /api/me`                           | always: who is signed in, or 401 |
| `GET /auth/providers`, `/auth/login/{id}`, `/auth/callback/{id}`, `POST /auth/logout` | sign-in |
| `GET /api/search`                       | always   |
| `GET /api/systems`, `/api/systems/{name}` | always |
| `GET /api/systems/{name}/topology`      | always   |
| `GET /api/components`, `/api/components/{name}` | always |
| `GET /api/messages`, `/api/messages/{name}` | always |
| `GET /api/systems/{name}/docs`          | `docs`   |
| `GET /healthz`, `/readyz`               | liveness, and readiness (Postgres answers) |
| `GET /…`                                | the UI, when `ATRIUM_WEB_DIR` is set |

Everything else under `/api` needs a session (401 without one, 403 without a role).
Anything unknown under `/api` is a 404, as decision 0007 asks of a source that's off.

### Ingest

CI posts after a merge to the main branch. The system comes from the document;
posting the same system and commit again changes nothing (200 instead of 201).

```sh
curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/topologies \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer REDACTED" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "repository": "acme/order-flow",
    "commit": "4f2a9c1e…",
    "ref": "refs/heads/main",
    "document": { …the graph verb'"'"'s output… },
    "docs": [{ "path": "README.md", "content": "# Order flow…" }]
  }'
```

Only `topology.intropy.io/v1` documents are accepted. Docs from the repository root
named README.md and RUNBOOK.md are shown; other files are stored but not served.

## Image

The Dockerfile at the repository root builds one image with the API and the UI
(decision 0008): Node builds the UI, Go a static binary, and the result runs on
`gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot`. No shell, non-root, about 15 MB, fine with
a read-only root filesystem. Base images are pinned by digest.

```sh
task image        # build atrium:dev
task image:run    # run it on :8081 against the local Postgres
```

Multi-arch builds cross-compile instead of emulating:
`docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 .`

Distroless has no shell for a Docker `HEALTHCHECK`; in Kubernetes, probe `/healthz`
(liveness) and `/readyz` (readiness).

## Atrium Hub

```sh
task backend:hub:dev   # the hub API on :8090 (task dev:hub from the root adds the UI)
```

| Variable                   | Meaning                                                           |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ATRIUM_DATABASE_URL`      | Atrium's database, through a read-only user; the hub never migrates it |
| `ATRIUM_INTEGRATIONS_FILE` | integration declarations (0010), required; `demo/integrations.json` locally |
| `ATRIUM_INCIDENTS`         | `demo` for the demo incidents; unset turns incidents off          |
| `ATRIUM_SLUICIO_URL`       | the customer's Sluicio; each integration links to its messages    |
| `ATRIUM_ADDR`, `ATRIUM_WEB_DIR`, `ATRIUM_LOG_FORMAT` | as for Atrium                          |
| `ATRIUM_AUTH_CONFIG`, `ATRIUM_SESSION_KEY`, `ATRIUM_AUTH` | as for Atrium, with its own app registration; locally `dev/auth-hub.json` |

Its API names integrations and business systems only, never components; a test checks
that. Each integration carries links: its diagram in Revision (`revisionUrl` in its
declaration) and its messages in Sluicio, found by the integration ID its traces are
tagged with. The Sluicio URL scheme is a guess, in one function (`sluicioLink`). Incidents are restated per integration: an integration is hit as badly as the
worst-hit of its components, and incidents that touch no integration are left out.

## Layout

| Path                 | What                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `cmd/atrium`         | `atrium serve`, `atrium migrate` and `atrium seed DIR`       |
| `cmd/atrium-hub`     | Atrium Hub's API and UI                                      |
| `internal/hub`       | the hub's HTTP API                                           |
| `internal/integrations` | integration declarations, behind a swappable source       |
| `internal/incidents` | incidents, behind a source; `Demo` until incident.io is wired |
| `internal/topology`  | the document, decoded and validated                          |
| `internal/catalog`   | the projection: latest snapshots to systems, components, messages |
| `internal/store`     | Postgres, with migrations embedded and applied on start      |
| `internal/api`       | HTTP handlers, ingest auth, feature gating                   |
| `internal/auth`      | sign-in with OpenID Connect, sessions and roles (0011)       |
| `internal/features`  | the feature flags                                            |
| `internal/web`       | serves the built UI: client routes, caching, gzip            |

The catalog is projected on each read from the latest snapshot per system. With a
handful of systems per customer that takes a few milliseconds and keeps one place
that decides what a document means; projected tables can come when a query needs
them. `internal/catalog` is a port of the web mock's `src/mocks/project.ts` and
returns the same JSON, minus what needs a schema registry (versions, schema
documents, examples); a message's format comes from its contract's media type.

## Analysis: publishing topologies to Atrium from the CLI

**In short:** Atrium already has everything it needs on its side. `POST /api/topologies` accepts a `topology.intropy.io/v1` document plus `repository`, `commit`, `ref` and `docs`, authenticated with a bearer token. Posting the same system and commit twice is safe. The work is mostly a new CLI command, and Atrium's CI step (decision 0003) then just runs that command.

### What exists today

| Side | What's there |
|---|---|
| Atrium | Ingest in `backend/internal/api/api.go`. `atrium seed` (`backend/cmd/atrium/seed.go`) is effectively a reference client. The token comes from `ATRIUM_INGEST_TOKEN`. |
| Atrium decisions | 0001: the CLI and Atrium share no code, and the topology document is the contract between them. 0003: "CI builds the host, runs `graph`, posts", as a step in the workflows intropy-templates generates. That step doesn't exist yet. I found no generated CI workflows in intropy-templates. |
| CLI | `topology.RunGraph` (`internal/topology/graph.go:28`) builds and runs the host. `template.ListSystemHosts` finds hosts. `internal/git` has `HEAD`, `Status`, `RemoteURL` and `DefaultBranch`. Config contexts layer flag, then env, then context, then global settings (`internal/config/config.go:219`). |

### Recommended shape

**Command: `intropy sys publish`**, under the existing `sys` noun.
1. Find the system host. Use `--system`, or discover it from the working directory as `manifests inspect` does.
2. Refuse a dirty worktree. The snapshot is keyed on system and commit, so a dirty tree would store content under a commit that doesn't contain it.
3. Read the commit from `HEAD`, the ref from the current branch, and the repository (`owner/name`) from the `origin` URL.
4. Run `graph` **without `--development`**. That section holds local file paths, which shouldn't end up in a shared portal. `RunGraph` always passes the flag and returns a decoded struct, so add an option or variant that skips the flag and also returns the raw bytes. Atrium stores the raw document, so send exactly what the host printed. Decode it only to validate.
5. Attach `README.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` from the repository root.
6. POST. A 201 prints `published order-flow @ 4f2a9c1 to atrium.acme.example` on stderr. A 200 prints `order-flow @ 4f2a9c1 already published`. Exit 0 in both cases.

**Config**
- Add `atriumUrl` to `Config` and `Context`, with `INTROPY_ATRIUM_URL` and an `--atrium-url` flag. Add the flag text to `flagtext.go`.
- The token comes from the `INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN` environment variable only, never from the config file.

**Verb:** AGENTS.md defines `publish` as pushing an immutable artifact to an OCI registry. An Atrium snapshot is also immutable per system and commit, so the verb fits, but that AGENTS.md entry needs widening, with the reason written there.

**Templates:** the 0003 CI step becomes one line on merge to main:
```yaml
- run: intropy sys publish
  env: { INTROPY_ATRIUM_URL: ..., INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ATRIUM_INGEST_TOKEN }} }
```
The protocol logic then lives in the CLI, where it can be tested, rather than in YAML that every customer forks. Amend 0003 to say that the CI step runs the CLI.

### Gaps on the Atrium side to fix alongside
1. **"Latest" means "last received".** Atrium stores `ref` but doesn't use it to pick the current snapshot, so a publish from a feature branch replaces what main shows. Two fixes:
   - Atrium only treats default-branch snapshots as current.
   - The CLI refuses any branch other than the default unless given an explicit flag.
2. **Ordering.** Design.md already flags that backfilling an older commit makes it current. The CLI can send `committedAt` cheaply from git, and Atrium can order by it.
3. **Auth.** Today there is one shared ingest token per customer. That's fine for CI secrets. Handing it to developers' laptops is weak, so that question decides how far laptop publishing should go. GitHub OIDC is the later fix design.md mentions.

### Suggested order
1. CLI: `sys publish`, the `atriumUrl` config, and the `graph` variant without `--development`. Test it against `task dev` in Atrium, which uses `dev-token`.
2. Atrium: ref-aware current snapshot plus `committedAt`, and an update to 0003.
3. Templates: the publish step in the system-host CI workflow.

### Decision for you
**Should `sys publish` be CI-only in practice, or something developers also run from laptops?**
- **CI-only:** a shared token is fine, and the CLI can require the default branch strictly.
- **Laptops too:** we need per-user auth, or at least a guard against branch snapshots overwriting main.

I'd start CI-only and keep laptop use as a manual backfill from the default branch. If that works for you, I can start on step 1.
We will start with laptop only. We are finding our way and want to start as simple as possible

Laptop-only keeps it simple: a shared token in an environment variable, and no CI work for now. One guard is still worth having: refuse to publish from a branch other than the default branch. Atrium treats the last snapshot it receives as current, so publishing from a branch would replace what main shows. I'll start on step 1.

### Configuration

The GitOps repository is a per-user setting, read from
`~/.config/intropy/config.yaml` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/intropy/config.yaml`):

```yaml
gitopsRepo: git@gitlab.com:integrio/intropy/customers/acme/gitops.git
```

Override it with `--gitops-repo` or `INTROPY_GITOPS_REPO`; flags win over the
environment, which wins over the file. `git` and `kustomize` must be on `PATH`.

The same file can point scaffolding at a private template library:

```yaml
templateRepo: acme/intropy-templates
```

The value is `owner/repo` on GitHub — the library is fetched over the GitHub
API, so URLs and SSH remotes are rejected. Override it with `--template-repo`
or `INTROPY_TEMPLATE_REPO`, on `int create`, `sys create`, `template list`,
`template show`, and the `manifests` commands. Unset, the official library at
`integrio-intropy/intropy-templates` is used.

#### Customer contexts

Working across several customers means the settings above change together.
The same file holds them as named contexts, kubeconfig-style:

```yaml
organization: integrio
currentContext: acme
contexts:
  acme:
    organization: acme
    gitopsRepo: git@gitlab.com:integrio/intropy/customers/acme/gitops.git
  staging-eu:
    gitopsRepo: git@gitlab.com:integrio/intropy/customers/staging-eu/gitops.git
```

A context overrides only the top-level keys it sets; the rest fall through
to the file's defaults, so `staging-eu` above keeps the top-level
`organization`. Precedence is flag > environment > active context >

content.text:
I've added `intropy sys publish`. It publishes a system's topology from your laptop to Atrium, and it works end to end against a local Atrium. It's on branch `feat/sys-publish-atrium`; nothing is committed yet.

**Using it**
```sh
export INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN=…
intropy sys publish --atrium-url https://atrium.acme.example
```
- **URL:** you can also set it with `INTROPY_ATRIUM_URL` or as `atriumUrl` in a context in the config file. `intropy context show` now lists it.
- **Token:** it is read only from `INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN`. There's deliberately no config key for it, so it never ends up in a file that gets copied around.

**What it does**
1. Finds the system host. `--system` picks one when the workspace has several, the same way `manifests` does.
2. Refuses to run if:
   - the system's directory has uncommitted changes, or
   - HEAD isn't pushed to the remote's default branch. This is the guard from before: Atrium treats the last topology it receives as current, so publishing from a branch would replace what main shows.
3. Runs the host's `graph` verb without the development section, so paths from your machine don't leave it, and sends the output exactly as the host printed it.
4. Posts it with the commit, `refs/heads/<default branch>`, the repository as `owner/name` from `origin`, and `README.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` from the repository root.
5. Publishing a commit Atrium already has is not an error. It prints `order-flow @ 1e0958f is already published to …` and exits 0.

**Tested:** all of `go test ./...` passes, including new tests that use real git repositories and a stand-in Atrium. I also ran it against a real local Atrium, using a scratch copy of `intropy-bis/sandbox/order-flow`:
- The first publish was stored and the second reported "already published".
- Atrium's catalog showed the system, its docs and the right commit, with no development section stored.
- A wrong token gave a 401 that names `INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN`.
- A commit on a feature branch was refused.

**Other changes in the diff**
- I made `deploy.SelectHost` public so the new command can reuse host selection.
- I widened the `--system` help text that the `manifests` commands share to "system to act on…".
- `publish` in AGENTS.md now covers Atrium as well as OCI registries.
- README has a "Publish the topology to Atrium" section.

**Worth knowing**
- A wrong token is only discovered after the build, which can take a minute. Atrium has no endpoint for checking a token first.
- Atrium's ingest token is one shared value per install, so everyone who publishes needs it. That's fine for now; it's what CI or per-user auth would replace later.
- The local Atrium's Postgres container is still running from `task backend:dev`. Stop it with `docker compose down` in `intropy-atrium/backend`.

content.text:
Atrium doesn't issue tokens. You make one up: any long random string. Atrium is given that value, and it accepts any request carrying the same value.

**1. Generate a value**
```sh
openssl rand -base64 32
```

**2. Give it to Atrium.** The Helm chart reads it from a Secret. This is the setup used in `ci/production-values.yaml`:
```sh
kubectl -n <atrium-namespace> create secret generic atrium-ingest \
  --from-literal=token='<the value>'
```
```yaml
# values for the Atrium release
atrium:
  ingest:
    existingSecret: { name: atrium-ingest, key: token }
```
You can also put the value directly in `atrium.ingest.token` and the chart creates the Secret, but a Secret you manage yourself keeps it out of your values files. When neither is set, ingest is off and every publish fails with 503. Atrium reads the token only at startup, so restart the pods after you change the Secret.

**3. Use it on your laptop**
```sh
export INTROPY_ATRIUM_TOKEN='<the value>'
```

Locally, `task backend:dev` uses `dev-token`, which is what I used in the test run.

Since there's one shared token per install, keep it in a password manager rather than chat. To rotate it, update the Secret, restart Atrium, and send the new value to everyone who publishes.
